entities.summary:
Najaf, an ancient city located in central Iraq, serves as the capital of the Najaf Governorate and is one of the most significant centers of Shia Islam. Founded in the 7th century CE, it is situated approximately 160 km south of Baghdad and has evolved into a vital spiritual and political hub for Shia Muslims. The city is renowned for housing the Imam Ali Mosque, which is the burial site of Imam Ali, the first Imam in Shia belief and the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad. This connection to Imam Ali elevates Najaf's religious status, making it a pilgrimage destination for millions, further solidifying its role in Islamic history.

Throughout its history, Najaf has witnessed pivotal events, particularly during the Abbasid Caliphate (750–1258 CE), when it became a center for religious scholarship and jurisprudence. The city was home to notable scholars such as Al-Shafi'i and Al-Kufi, contributing to the development of Islamic law and theology. The 20th century brought further prominence to Najaf during the rise of Shia political movements in Iraq, especially after the 2003 invasion, when it emerged as a focal point for Shia political authority and identity in the post-Saddam era.

The legacy of Najaf is profound, as it has influenced the socio-political landscape of Iraq and Shia Islam worldwide. The city has become a symbol of Shia resilience and identity, impacting religious and political discourse in the region. Najaf's educational institutions have produced generations of clerics who have played critical roles in shaping Shia thought and practice. The city continues to be a center for theological debate and political activism, reflecting the evolving dynamics of Shia Islam in contemporary society.
